gold.caveat: Through 2024-12: World Bank monthly average of the London afternoon fixing (99.5% fine, nominal USD per troy ounce). After that month the World Bank file used here has not been updated, so the tail is the COMEX front-month gold futures monthly close (Yahoo GC=F), not the London fix. The two were checked on their overlap and were not rescaled.

sources.name: World Bank Commodity Markets, monthly prices (pink sheet)
Yahoo Finance GC=F COMEX gold futures, monthly close

btc.caveat: Monthly average of the daily Coinbase bitcoin price on FRED. Earlier bitcoin prints are not used.

recipe.name: Dried beans, any type
recipe.energyNote: USDA black beans, mature seeds, raw, 341 kcal/100 g, as a stand-in for the BLS any-type dried-bean price. Other dry beans are about 337–347 kcal/100 g.

recipe.name: White all-purpose flour
recipe.energyNote: USDA wheat flour, all-purpose, enriched, 364 kcal/100 g.

recipe.name: White pan bread
recipe.energyNote: USDA white bread, commercially prepared, 266 kcal/100 g.

recipe.name: Dry spaghetti and macaroni
recipe.energyNote: USDA dry enriched pasta, 371 kcal/100 g.

recipe.name: Eggs, grade A large
recipe.energyNote: USDA whole raw egg, 143 kcal/100 g, times a 50 g large egg, times 12.

recipe.name: Ground chuck, 100% beef
recipe.energyNote: USDA raw ground beef, 80% lean / 20% fat, 254 kcal/100 g, used as a proxy for BLS ground chuck.

recipe.name: Whole fresh chicken
recipe.energyNote: USDA broiler meat and skin, raw, 215 kcal/100 g (about NDB 171447). Applied to purchase weight; bone is not removed, so edible kcal are lower.

recipe.name: Sliced bacon
recipe.energyNote: USDA pork, cured, bacon, unprepared, 393 kcal/100 g (FDC 168277).

recipe.name: Field-grown tomatoes
recipe.energyNote: USDA red tomatoes, raw, 18 kcal/100 g.

recipe.name: Whole milk
recipe.energyNote: USDA whole milk, 3.25% fat, 61 kcal/100 g. One cup taken as 244 g, 16 cups in a gallon.

omitted.name: Car / food week
omitted.reason: No long public dollar series for the average U.S. new-car transaction price was found. CPI new vehicles is an index and is on the life-cost strip. Dividing that index by the food-week dollar cost would mix units, so the ratio is omitted.

omitted.name: Existing-home median in gold or bitcoin
omitted.reason: FRED HOSMEDUSM052N did not return a long history from the public CSV endpoint during this refresh (a short recent sample only). House charts use the Census median sales price of new houses (MSPNHSUS).

omitted.name: Official USDA food-plan dollar cost
omitted.reason: USDA food plans are published as spreadsheets and PDFs, not as a stable keyless series. The food week is an explicit BLS-price reconstruction.

life.title: WTI crude oil
life.caveat: Cushing, Oklahoma spot. Monthly average of daily prices. The newest month is partial until EIA finishes it.

life.title: Regular gasoline
life.caveat: U.S. regular, all formulations, retail. Weekly EIA prices averaged by month.

life.title: Diesel
life.caveat: U.S. diesel sales price. Weekly EIA prices averaged by month.

life.title: Residential electricity
life.caveat: U.S. city-average price per kilowatt-hour. Not a particular utility bill.
life.source: BLS average price via FRED APU000072610

life.title: Water, sewer, and trash*
life.caveat: Not a gallon of water and not a water bill. CPI-U for water, sewer, and trash collection together, seasonally adjusted. U.S. city average. The series begins in 1997.

life.title: Food week*
life.caveat: A fixed non-organic basket of about 1,966 kcal/day (13,765 kcal in the week), built from BLS city-average shelf prices. Not an official USDA Food Plan and not a household grocery bill. No organic premium. Whole-chicken calories are overstated because the price includes bone. Dried beans stand in for rice: the white-rice city average was unpublished for two years (2000–2002), and navel-orange prices are seasonal, so those series were left out rather than filled in. A month is blank when any ingredient was not published. Nothing is carried forward. The basket starts July 1995, when the whole-milk gallon series starts.
life.source: BLS average prices via FRED, recipe in the sources section

life.title: New vehicles*
life.caveat: Not a sticker price and not the average transaction price. CPI-U new vehicles, seasonally adjusted, 1982–84 = 100. A long public dollar series for the average new car was not available, so the car/food-week ratio is omitted.

life.title: Televisions*
life.caveat: Not the shelf price of a flat screen. CPI-U televisions, not seasonally adjusted, December 2024 = 100 after the 2026 rebase. Quality-adjusted, and the history includes tube sets before flat panels. Gold and bitcoin views are index points per ounce or coin, not a TV’s price tag.

charts.title: U.S. new-house price in gold
charts.subtitle: Median sales price of new houses sold, divided by that month’s gold price. Dollars cancel. New houses, not the existing-home median.
charts.source: Census/HUD via FRED MSPNHSUS, divided by the gold series below.

charts.title: U.S. new-house price in bitcoin
charts.subtitle: Same median new-house price, divided by the monthly average Coinbase bitcoin price. Starts December 2014, the first month of FRED CBBTCUSD. Log scale so the early years do not hide the recent level.

charts.title: Gold vs S&P 500
charts.subtitle: Both lines start at 100 in 1985-01, their first shared month. This is a price index, not a total-return index: dividends are not in the S&P line. Gold is the spliced series described in Sources.
charts.source: World Bank / Yahoo GC=F gold, and Yahoo Finance ^GSPC monthly close.

charts.title: Bitcoin purchasing power vs the dollar
charts.subtitle: Dollars one bitcoin exchanged for on Coinbase, monthly average, log scale. Nominal: this is not adjusted by CPI. It is the purchasing power of a bitcoin measured in dollars.

charts.title: New house vs household income
charts.subtitle: Average of that year’s monthly median new-house prices, divided by nominal median household income. A reading of 4 means the median new house cost four years of the median household’s pretax income. Income is annual and lags; a year is skipped until income is published and at least six house months exist.
charts.source: FRED MSPNHSUS and FRED MEHOINUSA646N (nominal, not the real 672N series).

charts.title: Food week / gold
charts.subtitle: Ounces of gold that buy one food week. Same basket as the life-cost strip.

charts.title: Gas / oil
charts.subtitle: Retail regular gasoline ($/gal) divided by WTI ($/bbl). A barrel is 42 gallons, so 1/42 ≈ 0.0238 would mean the gallon at the pump cost the same as a gallon of crude, with no refining, tax, or station margin. The dashed line is that benchmark, not a price forecast.
charts.source: FRED GASREGW ÷ monthly average of FRED DCOILWTICO.

charts.title: House / gold
charts.subtitle: Same series as the monetary chart above: troy ounces per median new house.

charts.title: House / bitcoin
charts.subtitle: Same series as the monetary chart. Log scale. Coinbase history only, from December 2014.

charts.title: Gold / S&P
charts.subtitle: Dollars per troy ounce divided by the S&P 500 price index. This is the reciprocal shape of “the index priced in gold,” kept here as the named ratio. Dividends are not included.

charts.title: Electricity vs wages
charts.subtitle: Kilowatt-hours one hour of pay buys. Pay is average hourly earnings of private production and nonsupervisory workers, gross, not household income and not after tax.

charts.title: Electricity vs CPI
charts.subtitle: CPI-U electricity and CPI-U all items, each rebased to 100 in January 1983 (inside the 1982–84 CPI base). A rising gap means the electricity index outpaced the all-items index after that date.
